title: Financial spreading: how lenders turn messy statements into numbers they can compare
summary: Spreading financials explained: a worked example, the ratios lenders compute, common errors, and how AI automates financial statement spreading for lenders.
body_markdown:
Picture an analyst at a community bank on a Monday morning. A machine shop has applied for a $300,000 equipment loan, and the file holds a tax return, two years of year-end statements from the shop’s accountant, a PDF of the latest quarter and several months of bank statements. The shop is fictional, and so is every number in this guide.


Nobody can say whether to lend from that pile yet. Each document names the same things differently. One page is in dollars and another in thousands. The figure the lender cares about most, the cash the business really generates, is not printed anywhere.


So the analyst opens a blank template and starts retyping, line by line, into rows that every borrower will share. That retyping is called spreading financials. It is the least glamorous step in commercial lending, it comes before every judgment that follows, and a mistake made in it can go into the credit memo unnoticed.


Quick answer


Financial spreading is the work of restating a borrower’s financial statements in one standard format, period by period, so a lender can compute ratios and compare one borrower with another.\[1\] Analysts have traditionally done it by retyping figures from tax returns, statements and bank records into a template.


Software can now read the documents and build the spread. The analyst reviews the exceptions, checks the conventions and makes the credit call.


Key takeaways


-


A spread is a borrower’s financials re-sorted into the lender’s own template, one column per period, so every borrower is read the same way.


-


The slow part is not the typing. It is deciding which row each line belongs in, and a wrong row moves the ratios: the same balance sheet gives a current ratio of 2.01 or 1.34.


-


Debt service coverage, the current ratio, leverage and margin trends all sit on the spread, so an error in it travels into every one of them.


-


AI can read the documents and build the spread. A person still decides the add-backs, the treatment of owner loans and what a falling margin means.


01


## What financial spreading means, in plain words


A spread is a grid. Down the side are standard rows: sales, cost of goods sold, operating expenses, cash, receivables, inventory, debt, equity. Across the top is one column per period. Every borrower’s numbers go into the same rows, whatever their accountant called them. The Risk Management Association, whose member banks submit their spreads for its annual industry benchmarks, defines it this way:


> “Spreading” is the process by which a bank transfers information from a borrower’s financial statements into the bank’s financial analysis spreadsheet program.\[1\]


The purpose is comparison. Once every borrower sits in the same rows, a lender can calculate ratios, set one year beside the next and set a borrower beside its industry. Bank examiners expect the same discipline: the OCC’s procedure for commercial loans tells them to analyze balance sheet and profit and loss items in the current and preceding statements and to determine whether any trend is favorable or adverse.\[5\]


For an SBA 7(a) loan above $350,000 the spread is a written requirement. The credit memorandum has to include a spread of the pro-forma balance sheet, a calculation of EBITDA, and ratio calculations for the current ratio, debt to tangible net worth and debt service coverage.\[3\]


Spreading is not credit analysis. Spreading produces the numbers. Analysis decides what they mean: whether margins fell because of a pricing mistake or a one-off supplier problem, and whether the borrower’s biggest customer is a risk. The spread is the input, and[credit analysis](https://www.kita.ai/credit-analysis-software) is the work that follows it.


02


## How a spread is built, in six steps


The steps are broadly the same whatever the loan type. What changes is the number of documents and entities.


1. 01


Gather the documents for every period you need


For an existing business on a standard SBA 7(a) loan, the lender needs three years of history plus an interim statement, and a current debt schedule that includes any shareholder debt. For smaller 7(a) loans SBA also requires two months of operating account statements, to confirm that every debt is in the coverage calculation.\[3\]


2. 02


Record each figure with its period and units


Note on every page the currency and whether figures are actual or in thousands or millions, whether statements are combined or consolidated, and whether they are audited, reviewed or compiled.\[2\]


3. 03


Map each line to a row in the template, splitting lumped lines


The same cost can hide in different places. Depreciation and interest often sit inside other lines, and have to be found and moved to their own rows.\[1\]


4. 04


Apply the lender’s conventions


Decide how related-party balances, prepaid expenses and restricted cash are classified, and spread “other” income and expense below operating income. Apply the same rules to every borrower.\[1,2\]


5. 05


Reconcile the spread to the source


The balance sheet has to balance, retained earnings should roll forward from one year to the next, and any cash flow the software generates should be compared with the one in the original statements.\[2\]


6. 06


Compute the ratios and read the trend


Calculate debt service coverage, the current ratio, leverage and margins, then set each period beside the one before it and look at the direction of travel.\[3,4,5\]


03


## A worked example: spreading one machine shop’s year


Everything here is invented for illustration. The numbers are round so the arithmetic is easy to follow, and the shop is not a real company.


### The income statement: the number you need is not printed


The accountant’s statement has eight lines, shown on the left of the figure. Two of them hide what a lender needs. “General and administrative” ($169,000) bundles $105,000 of everyday running costs with $64,000 of depreciation, which is the cost of equipment wearing out, not cash leaving the building. “Other expense” ($31,000) is interest on the shop’s loans, which the notes reveal.


The template wants those lines split apart. Once they are, a row appears that the accountant never printed: EBITDA of $159,000. That is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, a rough measure of the cash the business generates from operations. SBA defines the operating cash flow it uses for coverage as EBITDA.\[3\] Getting from the printed page to that row is most of what spreading is.

### The balance sheet: where the lender’s view parts from the accountant’s


As printed, the shop’s balance sheet looks healthy: $534,000 of current assets against $266,000 of current liabilities. Dividing one by the other gives the current ratio, which asks whether the business can pay what it owes in the next twelve months.\[4\] Here it is 2.01, and the OTS examination handbook calls 2 to 1 acceptable.\[4\]


A lender’s template is more cautious than an accountant’s, on purpose. RMA’s guide explains that bank spreads depart from accounting standards because a bank cares about one thing: what will turn into cash that can repay the loan.\[1\] Prepaid expenses, such as insurance paid ahead, will never become cash, so they move out of current assets. A $40,000 balance the owner owes the business is a related-party receivable whose repayment is discretionary, so that moves out too.\[1\]


The last move runs the other way. A $90,000 loan from the owner to the business is spread as a current liability unless it is formally subordinated to the bank, because an owner with early warning of trouble could call it in ahead of everyone else.\[1\]

Same balance sheet, same totals, two ratios. The spread’s version, 1.34, is the one that answers the lender’s question. Conventions also differ between lenders. The Export-Import Bank’s guidelines, written for foreign borrowers, say a shareholder loan formally subordinated to the debt the bank supports can be treated as equity in its performance standards.\[2\] The right treatment is a policy decision, and the point of a template is that it is applied the same way to every file.


04


## The ratios a lender reads off the spread


Once the spread is built, the arithmetic is quick. Each calculation is only as good as the rows beneath it.


Margins ask how much of each sales dollar survives. The shop’s gross margin, which is sales less direct costs divided by sales, fell from 34.3% to 33.2% while sales grew almost 10%, from $1,675,000 to $1,840,000. Its EBITDA margin slipped from 9.3% to 8.6%. The shop is growing and earning less on each job, and that only shows because both years sit in the same rows.


Leverage asks how much of the business runs on borrowed money. It is total liabilities divided by equity, and the OTS handbook notes that the higher it is, the greater the risk, though what counts as acceptable depends on the business.\[4\] The shop’s is 2.42, or $2.42 of liabilities for every dollar of equity. The same handbook says ratios are best judged against the company’s own prior years and similar businesses.\[4\]


Debt service coverage tests the main source of repayment, which SBA says is the applicant’s cash flow, not the sale of collateral.\[3\] It asks whether operating cash flow covers the loan payments: EBITDA divided by the principal and interest due on all of the business’s debt, including the new loan. That is SBA’s definition.\[3\]


The shop owes $48,000 of principal and $31,000 of interest on its existing debt in the coming year, and a $300,000 loan at 9% over ten years adds about $45,600 a year. Debt service is $124,600, so coverage is $159,000 divided by $124,600, or 1.28.


SBA sets the minimum at 1.10 for a 7(a) Small loan, which covers loans up to $350,000, and at 1.15 for a larger standard 7(a) loan. A standard loan also needs 1:1 on a global basis, which takes in the cash flow of any affiliated business.\[3\]


At 1.28 the shop clears both lines with a thin cushion. A fall of about 10% in EBITDA would put coverage under 1.15, and about 14% under 1.10, which is why the margin trend above matters.


Ratios computed from the machine shop spread Ratio The question it answers How it is computed Machine shop


Gross margin How much of each sales dollar is left after direct costs? Gross profit ÷ sales 33.2% (34.3% the year before)


EBITDA margin How much operating cash does each sales dollar produce? EBITDA ÷ sales 8.6% (9.3% the year before)


Current ratio Can the business pay what it owes in the next twelve months? Current assets ÷ current liabilities\[4\] 1.34 as spread (2.01 as printed)


Leverage How much of the business runs on borrowed money? Total liabilities ÷ equity\[4\] 2.42


Debt service coverage Does operating cash flow cover the loan payments? EBITDA ÷ principal and interest due on all business debt, including the new loan\[3\] 1.28


Notice the chain. Every ratio sits on a row the spread created, so a line placed in the wrong row does not make one wrong number. It makes several.


05


## Where spreading goes wrong


Many spreading errors are not typos. They are a line in the wrong row, or a row quietly missing. On the shop’s file, three plausible mistakes would each have changed the answer:


How three spreading mistakes change the debt service coverage ratio What the spread does The arithmetic Coverage


Right answer: EBITDA over all debt service $159,000 ÷ $124,600 1.28


Using profit instead of EBITDA Depreciation and interest are never added back: $64,000 ÷ $124,600 0.51


Leaving depreciation inside general and administrative costs A non-cash cost is treated as cash leaving: $95,000 ÷ $124,600 0.76


Leaving the new loan out of debt service Only today’s payments are counted: $159,000 ÷ $79,000 2.01


The published guidance names more. Each is easy to make and hard to see in a finished spread:


-


**Mixed units.** EXIM tells analysts to mark every page with the currency and whether the figures are actual, thousands or millions.\[2\]


-


**An overdraft as negative cash.** Cash should be zero and the overdraft shown as a liability.\[2\]


-


**Totals that do not tie out.** If retained earnings do not reconcile from one year to the next, the difference has to be found and explained, not left as a plug.\[2\]


-


**Related-party items spread as trade items.** A receivable from an affiliate is not a receivable from a customer, and it changes the turnover ratios.\[1\]


-


**Autopilot.** RMA says spreading should not be a mechanical exercise on “autopilot”, and that any exception to the lender’s standard should be explained so the approver knows.\[1\]


06


## How AI automates spreading, and what still needs a person


Look back at the six steps and notice which ones need judgment. Reading the pages, mapping the lines and doing the arithmetic are mechanical. Deciding how to treat an owner loan, which add-backs are fair and what a falling margin means is not.


Automation follows that split. Software reads the documents, including scans and photos, places each line in the template, ties out the totals, computes the ratios and keeps a link from each figure to the page it came from. The analyst’s time moves from retyping to reviewing: checking the flagged items and the conventions, then deciding.

A schematic of the workflow, not a measurement of time or accuracy. White steps are done by hand, green steps by software, and the shaded step is the analyst's judgment, which stays with a person in both versions.


Manual spreading takes time, and the estimates come from vendors. One software vendor puts a straightforward borrower at two to four hours and says multi-entity files take considerably longer.\[6\] Treat that as a vendor’s estimate, not a measurement. The point is that the hours go on this step before any analysis starts.


Automation has limits too. EXIM warns that spreading software only picks up the changes it sees in the balance sheet, so stock dividends, revaluations and assets bought with debt will not appear correctly in a generated cash flow, and the output should be compared with the borrower’s own.\[2\] RMA’s rule that every spread must be thought out does not change because a machine built it.\[1\]

## Frequently asked questions


### What is financial spreading?


Financial spreading is restating a borrower’s financial statements in one standard format, period by period, so a lender can compute ratios and compare borrowers. An analyst takes figures from tax returns, year-end statements and bank records, places each one in the lender’s template, and the resulting spread feeds ratios such as debt service coverage, the current ratio and leverage. It is also called spreading financials or financial statement spreading.


### How do you spread financial statements?


Gather the documents for each period, record every figure with its period and units, map each line to a row in your template and split any lumped lines, apply your conventions for items such as related-party balances and prepaid expenses, reconcile the totals to the source, then compute the ratios and read the trend. The worked example in this guide runs all six steps on a fictional machine shop.


### What ratios do lenders calculate from a spread?


The core ratios are debt service coverage (operating cash flow divided by the principal and interest due on all business debt), the current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities), leverage (total liabilities divided by equity) and margin trends. For a standard SBA 7(a) loan, SBA’s procedures name the current ratio, debt to tangible net worth and debt service coverage among the ratios the credit memorandum must show.


### How long does financial spreading take?


It depends on the number of periods, the number of entities and the quality of the documents. One software vendor estimates two to four hours for a straightforward borrower and says complex multi-entity files take considerably longer, which is a vendor’s estimate rather than an independent measurement. Software that reads the documents removes most of the retyping, and the analyst’s time moves to review.


### Can AI automate financial spreading, and does it replace the analyst?


AI can read the documents, map each line to a template, tie out the totals and compute the ratios, so the spread arrives built rather than typed. It does not replace the analyst. How to treat an owner loan, which add-backs are fair and what a falling margin means are judgment calls, and the lender’s underwriter decides the loan. An automated spread should still be checked against the borrower’s own statements.
